We explore three different functional forms of the IMF with machine learning and statistical techniques, combining forward modeling of synthetic color-magnitude diagrams with simulation-based inference. We find that a single power-law IMF fails to reproduce the observed luminosity function and also deviates from the canonical Salpeter IMF. Our best-fit broken power-law and lognormal IMF parameters are consistent with the Milky Way within 68% confidence level, providing evidence that star formation at metallicities as low as [Fe/H]$\approx-2.4$ follows a similar IMF as in the Milky Way. By treating Boo I as a local relic analogous to a high-redshift galaxy with a stellar mass of $\lesssim10^5 M_{\odot}$ at $z\gtrsim6$, our results provide evidence for the universality of the IMF across both local and high-redshift environments.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRCAM resolved stellar data of the Boötes I ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, the authors find that the low-mass stellar initial mass function (IMF) at extremely low metallicity ([Fe/H]≈-2.4) is consistent with the Milky Way IMF, supporting IMF universality across environments and redshifts.
AI.motivation: The IMF's dependence on star-formation environment, especially at low metallicities and high redshifts, remains poorly constrained. Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs) are local fossils of high-redshift galaxies hosting old, metal-poor populations, offering a unique pathway to probe the sub-solar IMF in extreme environments.
AI.method: JWST/NIRCam resolved over 10,000 stars down to ~0.15 M☉ in Boötes I UFD. Three IMF functional forms (single power-law, broken power-law, lognormal) were tested using forward modeling of synthetic color-magnitude diagrams combined with simulation-based inference and machine learning techniques.
AI.result: A single power-law IMF fails to reproduce the observed luminosity function and deviates from the canonical Salpeter IMF. The best-fit broken power-law and lognormal IMF parameters are consistent with the Milky Way IMF at 68% confidence level, even at [Fe/H]≈-2.4.
AI.conclusion: Star formation at extremely low metallicities follows a similar IMF as the Milky Way. Treating Boo I as a local relic of a high-redshift galaxy (M⋆≲10⁵ M☉ at z≳6), the results provide evidence for IMF universality across both local and high-redshift environments.

title: Identifying group galaxies merging with massive clusters using machine learning
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 18 pages, 17 figures
summary: The environment plays a critical role in galaxy evolution, with galaxy clusters and their infall regions offering diverse conditions that shape galaxies before they enter the dense cluster core, a process known as ``pre-processing''. However, identifying environmental substructures, particularly galaxy groups in these transitional zones, remains challenging due to projection effects and ``fingers-of-god'' distortions. In this work, we present a supervised machine learning framework for classifying galaxies into three environmental categories: main cluster, group, and neither, using observable galaxy properties such as positions, line-of-sight velocities, and stellar mass. The model is trained on mock observations derived from cosmological simulations designed to replicate survey conditions and achieves an overall accuracy and class-size-weighted precision of 81%. The neither and main cluster populations are reliably recovered, whereas group galaxies remain the most challenging to identify, achieving 30% completeness and 76% purity. Within $1\times R_{200}$, classification performance is suppressed, but it improves beyond this radius, reaching 40% completeness and 80% purity. Resampling and thresholding strategies allow the model to be tuned toward either higher purity or higher completeness; in this study, we adopt first-past-the-post thresholding to emphasise purity. Model performance is consistent across cluster masses and dynamical states, and it outperforms both Friends-of-Friends and Gaussian Mixture Modelling. This flexibility makes it well suited to upcoming spectroscopic surveys of cluster infall regions, providing a robust statistical tool for disentangling environmental influences on galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: A supervised machine learning framework classifies galaxies into main cluster, group, and neither categories using positions, velocities, and stellar mass, achieving 81% overall accuracy; group galaxies are hardest to identify (30% completeness, 76% purity), and performance improves beyond R200, outperforming Friends-of-Friends and Gaussian Mixture Models.
AI.motivation: Environmental pre-processing in cluster infall regions is poorly understood because identifying substructures like galaxy groups is difficult due to projection effects and fingers-of-god distortions.
AI.method: Supervised machine learning trained on mock observations from cosmological simulations, classifying galaxies into three environmental categories using positions, line-of-sight velocities, and stellar mass, with resampling and thresholding for tuning purity vs. completeness.
AI.result: 81% overall accuracy and class-size-weighted precision; neither and main cluster reliably recovered; group galaxies achieve 30% completeness and 76% purity; performance improves beyond R200; consistent across cluster masses and dynamical states; outperforms Friends-of-Friends and Gaussian Mixture Modelling.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a robust statistical tool for upcoming spectroscopic surveys of cluster infall regions to disentangle environmental influences on galaxy evolution.

title: The DESIRED electron temperature relations in star-forming regions of the local Universe
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables (2 longtables online). Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: Aims. We present a homogeneous observational study of electron temperature ($T_{\rm e}$) relations between ionic species: $T_{\rm e}$([N II]), $T_{\rm e}$([O II]), $T_{\rm e}$([O III]), $T_{\rm e}$([S II]), $T_{\rm e}$([S III]) and $T_{\rm e}$([Ar III]), using 699 spectra of Galactic and extragalactic H II regions and local star-forming galaxies (SFGs). Methods. We use the DEep Spectra of Ionised REgions Database Extended (DESIRED-E), comprising more than 3000 spectra with direct $T_{\rm e}$ determinations, selecting those with at least two $T_{\rm e}$ diagnostics. We recompute electron density ($n_{\rm e}$) and $T_{\rm e}$ using updated atomic data and a consistent methodology. The resulting $T_{\rm e}$--$T_{\rm e}$ relations are analysed using orthogonal distance regression, quantifying total and intrinsic dispersions and comparing slopes with previous works and photoionisation models. Results. Relations involving low-ionisation $T_{\rm e}$ diagnostics show large intrinsic dispersions, especially for $T_{\rm e}$([O II]) and $T_{\rm e}$([S II]), likely due to sensitivity to $n_{\rm e}$ inhomogeneities, recombination contributions, and uncertainties. In contrast, relations using $T_{\rm e}$([N II]) show lower dispersions, indicating that this diagnostic provides a more reliable estimate of the low-ionisation zone temperature when only higher-ionisation $T_{\rm e}$ diagnostics are available, despite observational difficulties at low metallicity. Overall, slopes agree with model predictions, particularly for relations with low intrinsic dispersion, such as those involving $T_{\rm e}$([N II]) and $T_{\rm e}$([S III]). These results provide a robust empirical basis for estimating $T_{\rm e}$ when limited diagnostics are available.

AI.tldr: This study presents a homogeneous analysis of electron temperature (Te) relations among multiple ionic species using 699 spectra from Galactic and extragalactic H II regions and star-forming galaxies. Using the DESIRED-E database, the authors recomputed Te and electron density (ne) with updated atomic data. They find that Te([N II]) and Te([S III]) relations show low intrinsic dispersion and agree well with photoionization models, making them reliable for estimating low-ionization zone temperatures when other diagnostics are limited.
AI.motivation: To provide homogeneous empirical calibrations of electron temperature relations between different ionic species, enabling reliable Te estimates when only limited diagnostics are available, and to test these relations against photoionization models.
AI.method: Selected 699 spectra from the DESIRED-E database (containing >3000 spectra with direct Te determinations) that have at least two Te diagnostics. Recomputed ne and Te using updated atomic data and a consistent methodology. Analyzed Te–Te relations via orthogonal distance regression, quantifying total and intrinsic dispersions, and compared slopes with previous works and photoionization models.
AI.result: Low-ionization Te diagnostics (especially [O II] and [S II]) exhibit large intrinsic dispersions due to ne inhomogeneities, recombination contributions, and uncertainties. Te([N II]) relations show lower dispersions, providing more reliable low-ionization zone temperature estimates. Overall slopes agree with model predictions, particularly for relations with low intrinsic dispersion (e.g., Te([N II]) and Te([S III])).
AI.conclusion: The derived Te–Te relations offer a robust empirical basis for estimating electron temperatures when limited diagnostics are available. Te([N II]) is recommended as the most reliable proxy for low-ionization zone temperature when only higher-ionization diagnostics exist.

title: Impact of stellar population models on the estimated physical properties of galaxies
comment: 17 pages, 17 figures, Submitted to Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: Accurate estimates of fundamental physical properties of galaxies, such as star formation rates (SFRs) or stellar masses, are essential for testing and constraining models of galaxy formation and evolution. Spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling has become the standard method for deriving these quantities. However, the influence of the underlying stellar population synthesis (SPS) models on the inferred parameters remains poorly quantified. This work investigates how the choice of SPS models affects the estimation of SFRs and stellar masses derived from SED modeling. Four widely used SPS models are applied to a sample of 17 230 galaxies with spectroscopic redshifts, selected from recently published Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope photometric catalogs. SEDs are modeled using the Code for Investigating GALaxy Emission. The analysis is performed in two steps: (i) estimating galaxy properties with each SPS model, and (ii) employing synthetic catalogs to assess the relative impact of model choice on the recovered parameters. Systematic differences are found among the models, with stellar mass estimates varying by up to ~ 0.6 dex and SFRs by up to ~ 0.4 dex between certain model pairs. The choice of stellar population model introduces significant systematic uncertainties in derived galaxy properties. This dependence should be accounted for when interpreting SED-based measurements and comparing results across different studies of galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how the choice of stellar population synthesis (SPS) models affects star formation rate (SFR) and stellar mass estimates derived from SED modeling of 17,230 galaxies. Systematic differences of up to ~0.6 dex in stellar mass and ~0.4 dex in SFR are found across four widely used SPS models, highlighting significant systematic uncertainties that must be accounted for in galaxy evolution studies.
AI.motivation: Accurate estimates of fundamental galaxy properties (SFRs, stellar masses) are essential for testing galaxy formation and evolution models. While SED modeling is standard, the influence of underlying SPS model choices on inferred parameters remains poorly quantified.
AI.method: Four widely used SPS models were applied to 17,230 galaxies with spectroscopic redshifts from HST and JWST photometric catalogs. SEDs were modeled using CIGALE (Code for Investigating GALaxy Emission) in two steps: (i) estimating galaxy properties with each SPS model, and (ii) using synthetic catalogs to assess the relative impact of model choice on recovered parameters.
AI.result: Systematic differences were found among SPS models, with stellar mass estimates varying by up to ~0.6 dex and SFRs by up to ~0.4 dex between certain model pairs.
AI.conclusion: The choice of stellar population model introduces significant systematic uncertainties in derived galaxy properties, which should be accounted for when interpreting SED-based measurements and comparing results across different galaxy evolution studies.
